21.name: FTP
21.description: File Transfer Protocol (control). Legacy file transfer — often targeted by credential brute-force.

22.name: SSH
22.description: Secure Shell. Remote login service. The single most-attacked port globally via credential brute-force.

23.name: Telnet
23.description: Unencrypted remote shell. Still present on many IoT devices; relentlessly scanned.

25.name: SMTP
25.description: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Attacked for mail relay abuse and credential guessing.

53.name: DNS
53.description: Domain Name System. Probed for open resolvers used in amplification attacks.

67.name: DHCP (server)
67.description: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server side.

68.name: DHCP (client)
68.description: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol client side.

80.name: HTTP
80.description: Plain web traffic. Huge volume of probes for vulnerable web apps and misconfigured servers.

110.name: POP3
110.description: Post Office Protocol for mail retrieval.

111.name: RPCBind
111.description: Sun RPC portmapper. Used in UDP amplification attacks.

123.name: NTP
123.description: Network Time Protocol. Used in UDP amplification attacks.

137.name: NetBIOS-NS
137.description: NetBIOS Name Service. Legacy Windows service often probed by worms.

143.name: IMAP
143.description: Internet Message Access Protocol for mail retrieval.

161.name: SNMP
161.description: Simple Network Management Protocol. Probed for default community strings.

389.name: LDAP
389.description: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Used in CLDAP amplification attacks.

443.name: HTTPS
443.description: Encrypted web traffic. Probed for vulnerable applications behind TLS.

445.name: SMB
445.description: Server Message Block. Windows file sharing — famously exploited by WannaCry / EternalBlue.

500.name: IKE
500.description: Internet Key Exchange used in IPsec VPNs.

623.name: IPMI
623.description: Intelligent Platform Management Interface. Famously insecure, often left exposed.

1080.name: SOCKS proxy
1080.description: SOCKS proxy protocol — probed for open proxies.

1433.name: MSSQL
1433.description: Microsoft SQL Server. Targeted for credential brute-force.

1723.name: PPTP
1723.description: Point-to-Point Tunneling VPN protocol. Obsolete and insecure.

2222.name: SSH (alt)
2222.description: Alternative SSH port used by administrators hoping to avoid port-22 scanners. Now heavily scanned itself.

2323.name: Telnet (alt)
2323.description: Alternative Telnet port used by IoT malware like Mirai.

2375.name: Docker API
2375.description: Unauthenticated Docker daemon. Exploited to deploy cryptominers.

3306.name: MySQL
3306.description: MySQL database server. Targeted for credential brute-force and data theft.

3389.name: RDP
3389.description: Remote Desktop Protocol. The second most-attacked port after SSH. Favourite entry point for ransomware.

5060.name: SIP
5060.description: Session Initiation Protocol. Voice/VoIP signalling — scanned for toll fraud.

5555.name: ADB
5555.description: Android Debug Bridge. Exposed ADB devices get cryptomined within minutes.

6379.name: Redis
6379.description: Redis key-value store. Misconfigured Redis instances are heavily exploited.

6443.name: Kubernetes API
6443.description: Kubernetes API server. Probed for exposed clusters.

7547.name: TR-069
7547.description: Home router management protocol. Historically exploited to enslave consumer routers.

8080.name: HTTP proxy
8080.description: Common alternative HTTP port. Scanned for open proxies and misconfigured services.

9200.name: Elasticsearch
9200.description: Elasticsearch HTTP API. Misconfigured instances leak data routinely.

11211.name: Memcached
11211.description: Memcached. Famously abused in record-breaking UDP amplification DDoS.

27017.name: MongoDB
27017.description: MongoDB database. Unauthenticated instances are routinely wiped by ransomers.

49152.name: Ephemeral
49152.description: Start of dynamic port range — random return traffic often lands here.
